title: Phishing the THAAD contractors
review_note: Complaint PDF on justice.gov was unreachable from this environment; defense-contractor facts come from the DOJ release, partial affidavit OCR (nsarchive, paras 9, 14, 52, 59) and press coverage of the complaint. Closing claim about later fake-job campaigns rests on the CyberScoop 2020 report headline; THAAD deployment date from Newsweek. Spot-check before publish if desired.

scenes.label: A job offer from a rival
scenes.narration: [softly] It looked like good news. A recruiter from a competing defense company, reaching out with an opportunity. [short pause] Some of these messages even mentioned THAAD — the American missile shield being set up in South Korea. [serious] But according to the FBI, the recruiter was a fake. The message was bait. And the people who wrote it, the US government says, were working for North Korea.

scenes.label: The shield built to stop missiles
scenes.narration: [serious] THAAD stands for Terminal High Altitude Area Defense. In plain words, it is a system designed to shoot down a ballistic missile as it comes back down, just inside or just beyond the atmosphere. Its prime contractor is Lockheed Martin, one of the biggest defense companies in America. In May 2017, as tensions on the Korean Peninsula climbed, the system was deployed in South Korea. [short pause] And that made the people who build it a target.

visuals.query: THAAD interceptor launch Missile Defense Agency

scenes.label: Programmers in a Chinese port city
scenes.narration: To understand who was behind the emails, prosecutors point to one man: Park Jin Hyok. According to the FBI, Park was a North Korean computer programmer who worked for more than a decade for a company called Chosun Expo Joint Venture. On paper, it was a business. A team of North Korean programmers worked out of Dalian, a port city in northeast China, taking paid coding and IT jobs for outside clients. [cautiously] But the Justice Department calls Chosun Expo a front — affiliated with a North Korean hacking unit sometimes known as Lab 110, part of the country's military intelligence.

scenes.label: A crew with a reputation
scenes.narration: Security researchers have their own name for this crew: the Lazarus Group. And by 2016, it already had a long record. Prosecutors tie the same conspiracy to the hack of Sony Pictures in November 2014, launched in retaliation for the comedy The Interview. They tie it to the theft of $81 million from Bangladesh's central bank in February 2016. [pause] Now, the government says, the same people were turning toward something else. Not a movie studio. Not a bank. America's defense industry.

scenes.label: Doing their homework
scenes.narration: Before you can fool someone, you have to know them. According to the FBI's sworn affidavit, the subjects did their homework. Court-ordered records show that people using a North Korean internet address visited the websites of intended victims such as Lockheed Martin — while researching Lockheed personnel and sending messages to its employees. [short pause] Reporting on the complaint says the hackers' successful attacks were usually preceded by the same thing: careful reconnaissance of their targets, online and on social media.

visuals.text: …visit the websites of some of their intended victims such as Lockheed Martin

scenes.label: The recruiter who wasn't real
scenes.narration: The weapon was spear-phishing. Ordinary phishing is a wide net, the same scam sent to thousands. Spear-phishing is a message written for one person — personal, believable, built to get them to click a link or open a file. Here, the affidavit says, the subjects created email accounts in the names of recruiters or high-profile people at one defense company, then used them to send recruiting messages to employees at its competitors. [softly] It's a clever disguise. A job offer is flattering. It feels private. And it's exactly the kind of message you want to open.

visuals.text: fake recruiter → employees at rival contractors

scenes.label: THAAD in the message
scenes.narration: Some of those messages, according to the Justice Department, made reference to THAAD itself. And in July 2017, the security firm Palo Alto Networks reported a wave of booby-trapped documents disguised as job ads, aimed at employees of US military contractors and linked by researchers to the Lazarus Group. One fake posting, Newsweek reported, was for a management position involving the THAAD missile defense system. [serious] The timing was hard to miss. That same month, North Korea launched missiles on July 4 and again on July 28, testing its Hwasong-14 intercontinental ballistic missile.

visuals.text: Hackers target US military workers with fake job ads

scenes.label: The door that held
scenes.narration: So what did the hackers get out of Lockheed Martin? [short pause] According to the Justice Department… nothing. The attempts to break into Lockheed Martin's computer systems were not successful. [reflective] In a story like this, that is a rare ending. The government has not said publicly exactly what stopped them, how many messages were sent in all, or whether every other contractor on the list was as lucky.

visuals.text: Attempts to breach Lockheed Martin "were not successful"

scenes.label: Same fingerprints, different target
scenes.narration: But a failed break-in still leaves fingerprints. When investigators traced the defense contractor emails, they found them tangled up with the Sony case. Some messages used the same aliases and accounts seen in the 2014 Sony attack, sometimes accessed from North Korean internet addresses. And the malware carried the same distinctive data table found in the Sony malware, and in tools used against banks. [pause] Different targets. Same toolbox.

scenes.label: One hundred search warrants
scenes.narration: Building the case took years. According to the complaint, investigators filed about 100 search warrants to get into roughly 1,000 email and social media accounts. The result was an affidavit 179 pages long, sworn by FBI Special Agent Nathan P. Shields of the Los Angeles field office. [cautiously] It reads less like a spy thriller and more like a giant ledger — which account logged in from where, whose address sat in whose contact list, which login came from inside North Korea.

scenes.label: The name that slipped
scenes.narration: And somewhere in all that data, the cover slipped. The hackers used a fake persona, Kim Hyon Woo, across several email and social media accounts. Park, meanwhile, used his own accounts for ordinary Chosun Expo work in China. The FBI says the two worlds touched. The usernames shared a pattern. One account was saved in the other's address book. Only the Kim Hyon Woo account could open an archive stored in an account tied to Park. And both sets were reached from some of the same IP addresses — the numeric address every internet connection carries.

scenes.label: A lack of opsec
scenes.narration: Eric Chien of the security firm Symantec put it bluntly, calling it "a lack of opsec." Opsec is short for operational security — the discipline of keeping your real identity walled off from your secret work. Agents even found a résumé showing Park had been employed as a developer, listing skills that included Visual C++, a programming language Lazarus used to build many of its tools. [short pause] For a man accused of hiding behind fake names, his paper trail was remarkably real.

visuals.text: "a lack of opsec" — Eric Chien, Symantec

scenes.label: Charged, but out of reach
scenes.narration: On September 6, 2018, the Justice Department unsealed the charges: conspiracy to commit computer fraud and abuse, with a maximum of 5 years in prison, and conspiracy to commit wire fraud, with a maximum of 20. The complaint tied the same conspiracy to Sony, to Bangladesh Bank, to the attempts on US defense contractors — and to WannaCry, the 2017 ransomware that hit hundreds of thousands of computers and badly disrupted Britain's National Health Service. The Treasury also sanctioned Park and Chosun Expo. [serious] FBI Director Christopher Wray said: "We stand with our partners to name the North Korean government as the force behind this destructive global cyber campaign."

visuals.query: US Department of Justice building Washington

visuals.text: "…the force behind this destructive global cyber campaign."

scenes.label: The offer that keeps coming
scenes.narration: Park Jin Hyok has never been arrested. The United States has no extradition agreement with North Korea, and he appears on the FBI's Most Wanted list. North Korea denies involvement. [reflective] And the trick he is accused of helping run never really went away. In the years since, security researchers have kept reporting North Korean campaigns built on fake job offers aimed at defense and aerospace workers. [softly] So the next time a stranger offers you your dream job… read it twice. [short pause] If you like stories like this, subscribe to Breach Uncovered.

seo.youtube_title: How North Korea Tried to Hack the THAAD Missile Makers | True Story
seo.youtube_description:
How North Korea tried to hack the makers of THAAD, America's missile shield in South Korea, with fake job offers from recruiters who did not exist. The true story of the Lazarus Group's spear-phishing campaign against Lockheed Martin and US defense contractors, explained.

In 2016 and 2017, according to the US Justice Department, hackers working for North Korea sent spear-phishing emails to American defense contractors, including Lockheed Martin, the prime contractor for the THAAD missile defense system. The emails posed as messages from recruiters at rival companies, and some mentioned THAAD by name. The attempts on Lockheed Martin failed, but the digital fingerprints matched the 2014 Sony Pictures hack and the $81 million Bangladesh Bank heist.

The FBI's 179-page affidavit names Park Jin Hyok, a North Korean programmer who worked for a front company called Chosun Expo in Dalian, China. Reused email accounts, a fake persona and a real résumé helped investigators connect him to the Lazarus Group. He was charged in September 2018 and remains out of reach.
